Edgware.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of north-west London
s1loc: Edgware sits at the head of the Northern line in north-west London, a historic stop on the Roman Watling Street, now the A5, that ran from London to St Albans. Its marquee draw is the nearby RAF Museum London on the former Hendon Aerodrome, where hangars hold Spitfires, a Lancaster and a Sunderland flying boat across the story of the Royal Air Force, with St Margaret's parish church and the old coaching-inn frontages marking the town's long history along the road.

The leisure and activity layer keeps operators busy across the year. Canons Park, a Grade II-listed formal garden laid out for the Duke of Chandos and home to the King George V Memorial Garden, sits beside Edgwarebury Park with its lake and trails, while Stoneyfields Park offers play space and pitches. The Broadwalk Centre anchors indoor shopping and dining, and The Hive Stadium at nearby Canons Park, home to Barnet Football Club, draws home-fixture and event crowds through the seasons.

Heritage and culture run through the wider district. The Anglo-Saxon roots at Little Stanmore, the splendid St Lawrence Whitchurch where Handel served as composer for the Duke of Chandos, and the open spaces of Stanmore Common and Harrow Weald give the area a layered past. Belmont and the conservation streets around Edgware village, the synagogues and community venues along the Edgware Road, and the events calendar at the local parks fill the diary beyond the high street.

Underpinning it all is a hotel and serviced-stay trade serving visitors to north London and the film studios nearby, with a guide and day-trip scene reaching across the suburbs. Edgware Underground station puts the West End within half an hour, and the A5, A41 and M1 funnel traffic north, so operators handle stopover trade as well as visitors heading for the studios at Borehamwood, Harrow on the Hill and the Hertfordshire countryside on the town's doorstep.

Bury.region: Bury and the north of Greater Manchester
Bury.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of northern Greater Manchester
s1loc: Bury runs a strong visitor economy in the north of Greater Manchester, anchored by Bury Market, a chartered market trading since 1444 and famous for its Black Pudding stalls and the World Famous Bury Market draw that brings coach trips from across the region. The East Lancashire Railway, a heritage steam line from Bury Bolton Street through Ramsbottom and Rawtenstall, carries visitors through the Irwell valley, while the statue of Sir Robert Peel, the town's most famous son, stands above the centre.

The leisure and activity layer keeps operators busy across the year. Burrs Country Park on the River Irwell offers the Burrs Activity Centre with kayaking, climbing and high ropes, a caravan site and the steam railway halt, while Clarence Park and Whitehead Park give families green space. The Mill Gate shopping centre anchors indoor trade, and the family draws of the wider Irwell valley, with Ramsbottom and the East Lancs line's themed Santa and dining trains, fill the calendar through the seasons.

Heritage and culture run deep here. The Fusilier Museum tells three hundred years of the Lancashire Fusiliers' history through uniforms, medals and Victoria Crosses, while The Met arts centre stages live music, theatre and comedy at the heart of the town. Bury Art Museum and Sculpture Centre holds the Wrigley Collection of Victorian art, and the events calendar, from the Bury Light Night to Ramsbottom's festivals, gives the area a busy cultural diary beyond the market.

Underpinning it all is a hotel and inn trade serving market visitors, business travellers and walkers, with a guide and coach-tour scene built around the market and the steam railway. The Manchester Metrolink tram puts the city centre within easy reach, and the M66 and M60 link the town to the wider conurbation, so operators handle day-trip crowds as well as visitors heading for the West Pennine Moors, Holcombe Hill and Peel Tower on the town's doorstep.

Tamworth.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of south-east Staffordshire
s1loc: Tamworth carries a busy visitor economy in south-east Staffordshire, anchored by Tamworth Castle, one of the best-preserved Norman motte-and-bailey castles in England, set above the rivers Tame and Anker with its battlements, haunted tower and an Anglo-Saxon exhibition on the Kingdom of Mercia featuring items from the Staffordshire Hoard. The historic Castle Pleasure Grounds, the medieval Church of St Editha and the statue of Aethelflaeda, Lady of the Mercians, mark the town's standing as a former Mercian capital.

The leisure and activity layer is unusually strong for the town's size. The SnowDome is one of the UK's premier real-snow centres, with year-round skiing, snowboarding, tobogganing and an indoor climbing wall, while Drayton Manor Resort, a short drive out, packs in roller coasters, the Thomas Land family area and a 15-acre zoo. The Tamworth Castle grounds, the Snowdome's pool and activity offer, and the indoor venues around the town keep families and operators trading right through the year.

Heritage and culture run deep across the district. The Ankerside and town centre conservation areas, the restored Tamworth Town Hall built by Thomas Guy, and the Peel connection through Sir Robert Peel and Drayton Bassett anchor the heritage offer. The Assembly Rooms stage live music and comedy, the Moat House timber-framed hall sits beside the Lichfield Street quarter, and the events calendar, from castle re-enactments to seasonal markets, gives the town a steady cultural diary through the seasons.

Underpinning it all is a hotel and inn trade serving theme-park families, business visitors and stopovers, with a guide and coach-tour scene built around the castle, the SnowDome and Drayton Manor. Tamworth station sits on the West Coast Main Line and the cross-country route, and the M42, A5 and A38 meet near the town, so operators handle day-trip crowds as well as visitors heading for Lichfield Cathedral, the National Forest and the Staffordshire countryside nearby.

Chatham.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Medway Towns
s1loc: Chatham runs a strong visitor economy at the heart of the Medway Towns, anchored by The Historic Dockyard Chatham, an 80-acre maritime site billed as the world's most complete dockyard of the age of sail. Visitors board HMS Gannet, the Cold War submarine HMS Ocelot and the destroyer HMS Cavalier, walk the quarter-mile Victorian Ropery and tour the Command of the Oceans galleries, in a setting used for filming Call the Midwife and Bridgerton on the banks of the River Medway.

The leisure and activity layer keeps operators busy across the year. Fort Amherst, the largest surviving Napoleonic fortress in Britain, opens its tunnels, batteries and ghost tours, while Capstone Farm Country Park and the Riverside Country Park at Gillingham give families trails and watersports on the estuary. Dockside Outlet shopping, the Medway Park leisure centre and the indoor activity venues around the town keep families and visitors trading through the seasons.

Heritage and culture run deep here. The Charles Dickens connection, formed in his Chatham childhood and woven through Great Expectations, links the town to neighbouring Rochester's Dickensian festivals, while the Royal Engineers Museum at Gillingham tells the story of the Sappers through medals and the Victoria Cross collection. The Brook Theatre, the Command House quarter and the events calendar along the waterfront give the town a layered cultural diary beyond the dockyard.

Underpinning it all is a hotel and inn trade serving dockyard visitors, university crowds and business travellers, with a guide and coach-tour scene built around the maritime heritage and the wider Medway story. Chatham station and the High Speed link put London St Pancras within an hour, and the M2 and A2 follow the old Dover road, so operators handle day-trip crowds as well as visitors heading for Rochester Castle, the Kent Downs and the North Kent coast on the town's doorstep.

Paisley.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Renfrewshire
s1loc: Paisley runs a distinctive visitor economy as the largest town in Renfrewshire, anchored by Paisley Abbey, the medieval church known as the Cradle of the Royal House of Stewart for its links to the Stewart kings, with its restored choir, the Barochan Cross and famed stained glass. The town's grand Victorian heart, built on the Paisley Pattern shawl trade and the Coats and Clark thread fortunes, gives the centre a wealth of listed buildings rare for a town of its size.

The leisure and activity layer keeps operators busy across the year. Barshaw Park, a Victorian public park with a boating pond, walled garden and pets' corner, sits beside the green spaces of the Gleniffer Braes Country Park, with its viewpoints over the Clyde valley and waymarked trails. The Lagoon Leisure Centre brings pools and an ice rink, the Robertson Park and the indoor activity venues around the town keep families and visitors trading through the seasons.

Heritage and culture run deep here. The Coats Observatory, the oldest public observatory in Scotland, sits near the reopened Paisley Museum and Art Galleries with its world-class shawl and textile collection, while the Sma' Shot Cottages preserve a weaver's home and the story of the Sma' Shot Day celebration each July. The Paisley Arts Centre, the Town Hall concerts and the festival calendar, from the Spree to the Halloween fireworks, give the town a busy cultural diary year-round.

Underpinning it all is a hotel and guest-house trade serving airport visitors, business travellers and event crowds, with a guide and tour scene built around the abbey and the textile heritage. Paisley Gilmour Street station puts Glasgow minutes away, and Glasgow Airport sits on the town's edge with the M8 alongside, so operators handle airport and stopover trade as well as visitors heading for the Clyde coast, Loch Lomond and the Renfrewshire hills nearby.

Carlisle.region: Carlisle and the Cumbrian border country
Carlisle.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Cumbrian border city
s1loc: Carlisle, Cumbria's only city, runs a strong visitor economy as the historic capital of the border country. Carlisle Castle, built on a Roman fort site from 1092 and once prison to Mary Queen of Scots, dominates the skyline with its keep, dungeons and the Cumbria's Museum of Military Life. Carlisle Cathedral, founded in 1122 and the second-smallest in England, sits in the Historic Quarter beside the Tithe Barn, anchoring a city shaped by centuries of Anglo-Scottish warfare.

The leisure and activity layer keeps operators busy across the year. Bitts Park and Rickerby Park line the River Eden with riverside walks and play space, while the Sands Centre brings pools, a leisure ice offer and an events arena, and Talkin Tarn Country Park nearby offers rowing, sailing and lakeside trails. The Lanes shopping centre anchors indoor trade, and the watersports, climbing and activity venues across the wider district keep families and visitors trading through the seasons.

Heritage and culture run deep here. Tullie House Museum and Art Gallery, set between the castle and the cathedral, holds a near-million-object collection covering the Romans, the Border Reivers and Cumbrian art, while the Guildhall Museum and the Citadel towers mark the city's medieval past. The Sands Centre concerts, the Old Fire Station venue and the events calendar, from the Carlisle Pageant to seasonal markets, give the city a busy cultural diary beyond its fortress walls.

Underpinning it all is a hotel and inn trade serving border visitors, walkers and business travellers, with a guide and coach-tour scene built around the castle, the cathedral and Hadrian's Wall. Carlisle station is a major West Coast Main Line junction and the start of the scenic Settle-Carlisle line, and the M6 runs alongside, so operators handle gateway trade as well as visitors heading for Hadrian's Wall, the northern Lake District and the Solway coast nearby.

Crewe.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of south Cheshire
s1loc: Crewe carries a visitor economy in south Cheshire built on its railway fame, anchored by the Crewe Heritage Centre on the original site of Crewe Works, once the largest railway engineering works in the world. The centre holds the only surviving Advanced Passenger Train, working signal boxes, a miniature railway and the Wedgwood War Memorial, telling the story of a town the London and North Western Railway built around its great junction station and locomotive shops.

The leisure and activity layer keeps operators busy across the year. Queens Park, a Grade II-listed 45-acre Victorian park gifted to the town by the railway company in 1887, offers a boating lake, clock tower and bandstand, while the nearby Crewe Alexandra ground at Gresty Road draws crowds on home fixture days. The Crewe Lifestyle Centre brings pools and fitness space, and the indoor activity venues and the wider Cheshire countryside keep families and visitors trading through the seasons.

Heritage and culture run through the town and district. The Lyceum Theatre, the only Edwardian theatre in Cheshire, stages drama, musicals and pantomime, while Crewe Market Hall has been reborn as a food, drink and live-entertainment destination. The town's railway-built streets, the nearby Bentley Motors heritage on the town's edge, and the events calendar, from market festivals to seasonal fairs, give Crewe a cultural diary beyond its junction reputation.

Underpinning it all is a hotel and inn trade serving rail travellers, business visitors and stopovers, with a guide and day-trip scene reaching the wider county. Crewe station is one of the most important junctions on the West Coast Main Line, and the M6 runs close by, so operators handle stopover and gateway trade as well as visitors heading for the Cheshire salt towns, Nantwich, the Sandbach crosses and the Peak District fringe on the town's doorstep.
